newsitem.title: USA: Senate committee approves Medicare, Medicaid cuts.
newsitem.headline: Senate committee approves Medicare, Medicaid cuts.

text.p: The Senate Finance Committee Wednesday unanimously approved wide-ranging budget legislation that would force affluent seniors to meet higher Medicare deductibles and create a new children's health plan.
The mammoth measure, needed to implement a balanced budget deal between the White House and Congress, would gradually raise the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from the current 65.
In a last-minute move, the panel sliced a controversial pilot programme that would have allowed some seniors to set up tax-free medical savings accounts as a Medicare alternative.

In sharp contrast to the pitched political battles of two years ago, Democrats and Republicans were in accord on the $115 billion in five-year Medicare cuts and $13.6 billion in Medicaid spending trims contained in the legislation.
"We have ended up with an agreement that hopefully will have wide bipartisan support," Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Repubican, said.

Senior citizens' groups were not as pleased. The American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) opposed the higher Medicare deductibles and eligibility age and was angry the panel did not include $1.5 billion set aside in the budget deal to subsidise Medicare premiums of poor seniors.

"There are serious problems for us in the Senate bill," John Rother of the AARP said. "It's hard to defend all these tax breaks in the same (budget) that will not include only $1.5 billion low-income seniors."

While not outright opposing a provision that would force affluent recipients to pay higher Medicare deductibles, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the original budget deal had purposely avoided higher out-of-pocket costs for seniors.

"The balanced budget agreement was very carefully constructed and the more you inch away from the central elements of that plan the more you run the risk of seeing the agreement itself begin to unravel," McCurry said.

The committee voted 18-2 for an amendment by Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey forcing better-off senior citizens to meet higher deductibles before Medicare Part B doctor's coverage kicked in. House committees have not approved a similar plan and it was expected to be highly contentious.
The Part B programme is voluntary but nearly all seniors eligible for Medicare choose it. The current Part B deductible is $100 per year and the monthly premium is $43.80.

Under the bill, senior citizens with incomes $50,000 and above and couples with incomes $75,000 and above would face sharply higher deductibles. The deductible would rise to more than $500 a year at the $50,000/$75,000 income level, growing to more than $2,000 for the most affluent seniors.

Administration officials said it was unclear how the government would collect income data to implement the provision. The change will affect Medigap policies seniors buy to cover deductibles and other services not covered by Part B.

The committee also voted to trim to 100,000 a pilot programme that originally allowed up to 500,000 older Americans to open tax-free medical savings accounts rather than using the traditional Medicare programme.

The White House was upset that despite President Clinton's personal plea the committee defeated a plan to cover up to half the nation's 10 million uninsured children by expanding the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled.

After arm-twisting by Senate Republican leaders and governors, who wanted more flexibility to design their own programmes, the panel instead passed a $16 billion alternative allowing block grants to states to design their own programmes.

Most of the bill's Medicare savings came from slowing payments to managed care, hospitals and other health care providers. The bill would offer seniors a wider array of health choices and new preventive services.

Doctors and hospitals would have new power to band together to form their own health care networks. The bill included new financial incentives to attract managed care plans to hard-to-serve rural areas.
